opus-5.5.text:
I think it's going to be more gradual than a lot of the hype suggests, but also probably faster than the skeptics expect. The first real deployments, the ones where robots are actually doing useful work and not just demos, are going to be in fairly structured environments. Think factories, warehouses, logistics. These are places where you already have a lot of automation, the tasks are somewhat repetitive, and the environment is controlled enough that you can manage the safety side of things.

What's interesting is that the hardware has gotten quite good. Locomotion especially. A few years ago, getting a legged robot to walk robustly over rough terrain was a research problem. Now, with reinforcement learning in simulation and sim-to-real transfer, it's something many groups can do reliably. So I'd say locomotion is mostly solved for these use cases. The bottleneck now is manipulation and the higher-level intelligence: understanding the task, dealing with all the variation in objects, recovering when something goes wrong.

So my expectation is that in the next couple of years we'll see small pilot deployments, maybe tens or hundreds of robots at a time, doing fairly narrow tasks like moving totes, loading and unloading, simple machine tending. Then as the learning methods improve, both from simulation and from collecting real-world data at scale, the range of tasks will widen. Once you have a fleet out there, every robot is generating data, and that creates a flywheel.

Homes are a much harder problem. The environment is unstructured, there are people and kids and pets around, and the safety and reliability bar is very high. So I think household humanoids are further out, more like the end of the decade or beyond, at least for anything general-purpose.

The other thing people underestimate is the economics. A robot doesn't need to be as good as a human to be useful. It needs to be reliable enough and cheap enough that the math works out. As costs come down with manufacturing scale, that threshold gets easier to cross, and I think that's when you'll see things really accelerate.

r001.rationale: The candidate predicts small pilots “in the next couple of years,” but does not identify late 2026 or early 2027.

r002.rationale: It discusses manufacturing scale as a factor in robot economics, but does not say producing physical hardware will prevent a sudden spread comparable to ChatGPT access.

r003.rationale: It expects early useful deployments in factories, warehouses, and logistics, and says household humanoids are further out.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, that's the question everyone wants a clean answer to, and I don't think there is one, but I can tell you how I'm thinking about it.

The first thing I'd say is that the locomotion part is, to a large degree, solved. Walking, running, recovering from pushes, going up stairs, handling rough terrain, that's where my background is, and over the last few years sim-to-real reinforcement learning has made that pretty reliable. You train a policy in simulation with massive parallelism, add enough randomization, and the robot walks on the first try. That used to be a research result. Now it's close to an engineering routine.

But walking around is not useful work. Nobody pays a robot to walk. The value comes from manipulation, and manipulation is where we're much earlier. The reason is that the thing that made locomotion work, simulation, doesn't transfer as cleanly. Contacts with deformable objects, cloth, liquids, cluttered scenes, all of that is hard to simulate, so you can't just run a billion trials and expect it to carry over. People are compensating with teleoperation data, with large pretrained vision-language models, with combinations of the two, and it's progressing fast, but the robustness isn't at the level where you'd leave the robot alone for a shift.

So in terms of how deployment unfolds, I expect it to go in stages, and the stages are defined by how structured the environment is.

The first real deployments are in logistics and manufacturing. Tote handling, moving boxes between conveyors, machine tending, things where the task is repetitive, the objects are known, and the environment is somewhat controlled. That's where we're seeing pilots already, and I think over the next two or three years those move from pilots to actual paid deployments at small scale, with a lot of remote monitoring and human intervention behind the scenes. Most people underestimate how much of the early "autonomous" deployment will actually have a human in the loop somewhere.

The second stage is semi-structured commercial environments. Retail back rooms, hospitals moving supplies, hospitality. More variability, more people around, higher safety requirements. I'd put that further out, maybe five years before it's more than a demo, because safety certification for a hundred-kilo robot walking around humans is a real bottleneck that has nothing to do with machine learning.

And then the home, which is what everyone imagines when they hear "humanoid," is the hardest and the last. Every home is different, the tasks are open-ended, the cost target is brutal, and the tolerance for failure is very low. I don't think that's a several-years story. I think that's a decade-plus story, and it probably arrives through something that looks more like a product gradually gaining capabilities than through a general-purpose robot showing up fully formed.

Two other things I'd flag. One is hardware. Hands are still the weak point. Durability, cost, dexterity, we don't have a hand that's good at all three. The robots that get deployed first will be the ones that pick a narrow task and a simpler hand and just make it reliable. The second is that I'm skeptical of the idea that there will be one foundation model that makes all of this fall out at once. I think the progress will be real but it'll be incremental, task by task, and the companies that win are the ones that get into actual deployments early and collect data from the real world, because that's the thing simulation can't give you.

So the short version is: locomotion is done, manipulation is the frontier, and deployment will track how structured the environment is, from the warehouse outward. I'm optimistic, I just think it's going to look more boring than the demos suggest for a while, and then it won't.

r001.rationale: The candidate places small paid deployments in logistics and manufacturing two or three years out, not around late 2026 or early 2027.

r002.rationale: The candidate discusses hardware limitations such as hand durability and cost, but does not explain that manufacturing physical hardware will prevent rapid spread comparable to ChatGPT access.

r003.rationale: The candidate expects initial deployments in logistics and manufacturing, with home use described as the hardest and last stage.

astra-6.text:
I think it’s going to be gradual. The first deployments will probably be in fairly controlled environments, where the robot has a specific task and where you can adapt the environment a little bit to help it succeed. Think of moving objects around in a warehouse or doing a repetitive task in a factory. Even there, you need much more than a good demonstration. You need the robot to work reliably for long periods, and you need a way to recover when something goes wrong.

I would expect those deployments to start small, with people supervising and helping when necessary. As we learn where the systems fail, we can improve them and expand the range of tasks they can do. The important question is how much useful work you get relative to how much human intervention is required.

Homes are a much harder setting because there’s so much variation, and you’re operating close to people. So I’m optimistic that we’ll see humanoids doing useful work over the next several years, but I’d be cautious about equating that with a general-purpose robot that can walk into any home and do whatever you ask.

r001.rationale: The response expects useful deployments over the next several years but gives no prediction of late 2026 or early 2027.

r002.rationale: It discusses reliability, supervision, and human intervention, but does not say hardware manufacturing will limit the speed of adoption or compare it with ChatGPT access.

r003.rationale: It places early deployments in warehouses and factories and describes homes as harder, indicating industrial use will precede consumer settings.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it’s going to be gradual. We’ll first see robots doing fairly narrow tasks in environments where you can control a lot of the complexity—factories, warehouses, places like that. Even if the robot is a general-purpose platform, the first deployment might be moving a particular object from one place to another, over and over.

The challenge is getting from a compelling demonstration to something that works reliably for an entire shift. What happens when something is in the wrong place, or the robot drops an object? Can it recover, or does someone have to come and help? Those details really determine whether it’s useful.

So over the next several years, I’d expect more deployments, with people still providing supervision and handling exceptions. As the systems improve, you can expand the range of tasks and reduce how much intervention they need. Homes are much harder because there’s so much variation and you’re operating around people. I’m excited about that direction, but I’d be cautious about putting a precise timeline on it.

r001.rationale: The response expects gradual deployment over the next several years but does not predict practical value beginning in late 2026 or early 2027.

r002.rationale: It does not explain that manufacturing physical hardware will slow spread compared with access to ChatGPT.

r003.rationale: It expects early deployments in factories and warehouses and says homes are much harder, clearly placing industrial settings before consumer settings.
